title: A3 — High-performing databases
bodyMarkdown:
## High-performing databases

Exam task **3.3**. Task 2.2 already covered database high availability -- Multi-AZ instances compared with Multi-AZ clusters, read replicas, Aurora Replicas, Aurora Global Database, DynamoDB global tables, and RDS Proxy's failover role -- so this lesson refers back to those briefly and focuses on **performance**: picking the right engine and type, sizing storage and capacity, scaling reads, avoiding hot spots, caching, pooling connections, migrating engines, and choosing analytics over transactional processing.

### K01 -- AWS global infrastructure

An **AWS Region** is an independent geographic area built from multiple **Availability Zones (AZs)**, each one or more physically separate data centers with their own power, cooling, and networking, connected to the other AZs in the Region by low-latency links. Database performance depends on this geography in two ways: placing a database instance in the same Region (and, where possible, the same AZ) as the application that calls it keeps round-trip latency low, and placing read replicas in AZs or Regions near the readers who use them shortens the read path further. A cross-Region call to a database adds tens of milliseconds that a same-Region call does not.

**Exam tip:** "queries from users in a distant Region are slow" points to a same-Region (or cross-Region read replica) placement fix, not a bigger instance class in the original Region.

### K02 -- Caching strategies and services

**Amazon ElastiCache** is a managed in-memory data store that sits in front of a database to absorb repeat reads, cutting both latency (microseconds instead of milliseconds) and load on the database tier. Two caching strategies decide when data enters the cache. **Lazy loading** (cache-aside) only loads an item into the cache after the application asks for it and misses -- the first request for any item is always a slower cache miss that falls through to the database, and the cache can hold stale data until it expires. **Write-through** updates the cache every time the application writes to the database, so cached data is always current, at the cost of writing items to the cache that may never be read and slower writes. A **time to live (TTL)** on each cached item combines the two: it caps how long lazy-loaded data can stay stale and evicts write-through data that is no longer needed, and most production designs use lazy loading (or write-through) plus a TTL rather than either strategy alone.

**Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX)**, covered in full under K02/S05 below, is DynamoDB's own purpose-built, API-compatible cache and is a separate service from ElastiCache.

**Exam tip:** "the cache must never serve stale data after a write" points to write-through; "minimize what gets cached to only what's actually requested" points to lazy loading; a TTL is the fix when the question wants both.

### K03 -- Data access patterns

Design the database around how it is used, not just what data it stores. A **read-intensive** workload (a product catalog, a reporting dashboard) benefits from read replicas, a reader endpoint, or a cache in front of the database, because most of the load is duplicate reads of the same or similar data. A **write-intensive** workload (an ingestion pipeline, an order-processing queue) does not benefit from read replicas at all -- every replica still funnels through the same primary for writes -- and instead needs a larger instance class, provisioned IOPS storage, write sharding across partition keys (DynamoDB), or a queue in front of the database to smooth bursts. Mixed workloads often split into two data paths: a normalized, write-optimized transactional store and a separate, denormalized, read-optimized store or cache fed by that transactional store.

**Exam tip:** count how the question's request volume splits between reads and writes before choosing a fix -- adding read replicas to a write-heavy bottleneck does nothing for the write path.

### K04 -- Database capacity planning

Capacity planning differs by service, and the terms describing it are easy to mix up. An **RDS or Aurora DB instance class** (for example `db.r6g.xlarge`) fixes the vCPU, memory, and network bandwidth available to the instance, split into general-purpose, memory-optimized, compute-optimized, and burstable-performance (`db.t`) families -- burstable classes earn CPU credits during idle periods and can be throttled once those credits run out under sustained load. **Storage** is chosen and sized separately from compute: **General Purpose SSD (gp3)** is the default, cost-effective choice with a baseline of 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s independent of volume size, tunable upward for an extra charge; **Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2)** is for I/O-intensive, latency-sensitive transactional workloads that need a guaranteed, consistent IOPS rate higher than gp3 can provide, at a higher cost. RDS storage auto scaling can grow allocated storage automatically as data grows, within a maximum you set. **DynamoDB capacity** is expressed differently again, in read and write capacity units (or on-demand request-based pricing -- see K08/S02 below), not instance sizes or provisioned IOPS at all.

**Exam tip:** "needs a guaranteed, consistent IOPS floor for a demanding transactional workload" is io2; "cost-sensitive, broad range of workloads, occasional IOPS burst is fine" is gp3.

### K05 -- Database connections and proxies

A database engine caps how many concurrent connections it can hold open, and that cap is often reached long before compute or storage becomes the bottleneck -- typically because a fleet of short-lived clients (Lambda functions, a busy web tier) each open and close their own connection per request. **Amazon RDS Proxy** sits between the application and an RDS or Aurora database, pooling and multiplexing many client-side connections onto a much smaller number of actual database connections, which both prevents connection exhaustion and reduces the CPU and memory overhead of opening new database connections repeatedly. RDS Proxy also improves failover behavior (task 2.2, K09), but the performance angle here is purely connection efficiency: an application under RDS Proxy can serve far more concurrent short-lived clients than the same instance could serve directly.

**Exam tip:** "the database is rejecting connections or timing out under a spike in short-lived clients, even though CPU and storage look fine" is a connection-pooling problem -- add RDS Proxy rather than resizing the instance.

### K06 -- Database engines with appropriate use cases

Choosing an engine is a migration decision as much as a feature decision. A **homogeneous migration** moves data between two databases running the same engine (Oracle to Oracle, MySQL to Aurora MySQL) -- the schema, data types, and code carry over largely unchanged, so **AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS)** alone can migrate the data with minimal downtime. A **heterogeneous migration** moves data between two different engines (Oracle to Aurora PostgreSQL, SQL Server to MySQL) -- because the schema, stored procedures, and data types differ, this is a two-step process: the **AWS Schema Conversion Tool (AWS SCT)** first converts the source schema and application SQL to the target engine's dialect, and only then does AWS DMS migrate and, optionally, continuously replicate the data. Skipping SCT on a heterogeneous migration is the classic exam distractor -- DMS moves data, it does not rewrite schemas or stored procedures.

**Exam tip:** "different source and target engines" always pairs AWS SCT (schema first) with AWS DMS (data second); "same engine on both ends" needs AWS DMS alone.

### K07 -- Database replication

A **read replica** is an asynchronous, read-only copy of a source database, created to scale read throughput horizontally by moving read traffic off the primary instance -- it is not, by itself, a high-availability feature, though it can be manually promoted to a standalone writable instance during a disaster (task 2.2). **RDS read replicas** can be created within the same Region or across Regions, and RDS for MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL, Oracle, and SQL Server all support them, each with some engine-specific limits. **Aurora Replicas** (task 2.2, K06) go further for performance: because they share the primary's underlying cluster storage volume rather than copying data, replica lag is typically single-digit milliseconds, an order of magnitude tighter than a standard RDS read replica's asynchronous lag, and a cluster can run up to 15 of them behind a single **reader endpoint** that load-balances connections across whichever replicas are currently healthy.

**Exam tip:** "read replica" scales reads; it is a performance tool first and a DR tool only as a manual, secondary use -- don't confuse it with Multi-AZ automatic failover (task 2.2, K06).

### K08 -- Database types and services

Match the data model to the purpose-built AWS service rather than forcing every workload into one engine:

- **Relational (SQL)** -- structured rows and columns with joins and ACID transactions. **Amazon RDS** runs MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server, and Db2 as managed instances; **Amazon Aurora** is AWS's own MySQL- and PostgreSQL-compatible engine, built for higher throughput and the scaling features in K06/K07/S04 above.
- **Key-value** -- simple lookups by a unique key, at very high scale and low, consistent latency. **Amazon DynamoDB** is AWS's serverless key-value (and document) database, billed by on-demand requests or provisioned, auto-scalable capacity units (S02 below).
- **Document** -- JSON-like documents queried by content, not just key. **Amazon DocumentDB** (with MongoDB compatibility) and DynamoDB's own document support both fit here.
- **In-memory** -- sub-millisecond reads for caching or ephemeral state. **Amazon ElastiCache** (K02 above) and **Amazon MemoryDB** (a durable, Valkey/Redis-compatible primary database, not just a cache) both serve this role.
- **Graph** -- traversing many-to-many relationships (social graphs, fraud rings, recommendations). **Amazon Neptune** stores nodes and edges and queries them with openCypher or Gremlin.
- **Time series** -- timestamped metrics ingested at high volume and queried by time range. **Amazon Timestream** is AWS's purpose-built time-series database family, but its original LiveAnalytics variant **closed to new customers on 6/20/25**; AWS now points new customers to **Amazon Timestream for InfluxDB** instead, so treat "Timestream for LiveAnalytics" as a legacy exam answer, not a current recommendation.
- **Wide-column** -- rows with a very large, variable number of columns, accessed with a Cassandra-style query language. **Amazon Keyspaces (for Apache Cassandra)** is the managed, serverless equivalent.

Aurora Serverless (K06/S04) and DynamoDB on-demand mode both illustrate the broader **serverless database** pattern: capacity scales automatically, including down to zero for Aurora Serverless, and billing follows actual usage instead of a fixed provisioned size.

**Exam tip:** when a scenario names its access pattern ("simple key lookups at massive scale", "traverse relationships between entities", "query documents by field"), match it directly to the service in this list rather than defaulting to RDS for everything.

### S01 -- Configuring read replicas to meet business requirements

Turn a stated read bottleneck into a replica configuration: add same-Region read replicas to offload reporting or analytics queries from the primary; add cross-Region read replicas to serve geographically distant readers with lower latency (and as a DR starting point, task 2.2); route the application's read traffic to the replica endpoint(s) explicitly for RDS, or to the single **reader endpoint** for Aurora so new replicas join the pool transparently; and monitor replica lag, since a replica that falls too far behind can return noticeably stale data to read-only clients. Promoting a replica breaks replication permanently and should be reserved for failover, not routine scaling.

**Exam tip:** "reporting queries are slowing down the production writer" is solved by adding a read replica and pointing the reporting tool at it, not by resizing the writer instance.

### S02 -- Designing database architectures

Assemble the pieces above into one design by asking, in order: what data model does the access pattern need (K08); how many concurrent reads and writes does it generate, and in what ratio (K03); does the write volume or item size demand instance resizing, gp3 versus io2 storage, or DynamoDB capacity mode and partition key changes (K04); would a cache in front of the database remove repeat load (K02, S05); would read replicas or Aurora Replicas remove read load from the writer (K07, S01); and does a connection-heavy client tier need RDS Proxy (K05)? For DynamoDB specifically, capacity comes in two modes: **on-demand** bills per request and scales instantly with no capacity planning -- the default, recommended starting point for most workloads and well suited to unpredictable or spiky traffic -- while **provisioned capacity** (optionally with **DynamoDB auto scaling** adjusting it within limits you set) costs less for steady, predictable traffic you can forecast. Provisioned or on-demand, throughput is still divided across partitions by the partition key, so **partition key design** matters either way: a key with too few distinct values, or one where most traffic lands on a small number of values, creates a **hot partition** that throttles requests well before the table's total capacity is exhausted. A **global secondary index (GSI)** has its own partition key (and optional sort key) different from the base table's, can be added or removed at any time, and is eventually consistent; a **local secondary index (LSI)** shares the base table's partition key but uses a different sort key, must be created when the table is created, and can be read with strong consistency.

**Exam tip:** "one item value gets almost all the traffic and throttles even though the table has plenty of provisioned capacity" is a hot partition from poor key design -- fix the key, not the capacity; "need to query by a completely different attribute, added after the table already existed" is a GSI, not an LSI.

### S03 -- Determining an appropriate database engine

Within the relational family, engine choice usually comes down to licensing, compatibility, and feature needs rather than raw performance: **MySQL** and **MariaDB** are common open-source choices for standard web-application workloads and are wire-compatible with tools built for either; **PostgreSQL** adds richer data types, extensions, and stricter SQL standards compliance, and is the engine of choice when an application needs those extensions or was already written against PostgreSQL; **Oracle** and **SQL Server** fit workloads with existing licenses, stored procedures, or vendor-specific features that must carry over unchanged (often requiring the heterogeneous migration path from K06 if moving off them); and **Amazon Aurora** (MySQL- or PostgreSQL-compatible) is the default recommendation when an application is compatible with either open-source engine and wants Aurora's higher throughput, storage auto scaling, and up to 15 low-lag replicas without changing drivers or SQL. Move to a NoSQL engine (K08) instead of a relational one when the access pattern is key lookups, documents, graphs, or time series rather than joined, transactional rows.

**Exam tip:** "already using PostgreSQL-specific extensions" or "needs stored procedures from an existing SQL Server database unchanged" rules out a same-family swap; "open to either open-source SQL dialect and wants the most throughput and read scaling" points to Aurora.

### S04 -- Determining an appropriate database type

Translate a scenario's shape directly into K08's service list: an e-commerce order table with joins between customers, orders, and line items is relational (RDS or Aurora); a shopping-cart or session store keyed by a single ID at massive, unpredictable scale is DynamoDB; a product catalog queried by many different nested fields is a document store; a leaderboard or session cache needing sub-millisecond reads is ElastiCache or MemoryDB; a "people you may know" or fraud-ring feature that walks relationships is Neptune; and a workload that scales unpredictably, including down to zero between bursts, is Aurora Serverless (relational) or DynamoDB on-demand (key-value) rather than a fixed-size provisioned instance. For Aurora specifically, choose **Aurora Serverless** when traffic is intermittent or hard to forecast and **Aurora provisioned** instances when traffic is steady enough to size and hold a fixed instance class efficiently.

**Exam tip:** the fastest way to eliminate wrong answers on a "which database" question is to name the access pattern (key lookup, document, graph, joined transactional rows, time series) first and let that pick the type -- then let cost and traffic shape pick the specific mode or class.

### S05 -- Integrating caching to meet business requirements

Add a cache where the same data is read far more often than it changes: **ElastiCache** in front of a relational database absorbs repeat read-heavy queries (K02) using lazy loading, write-through, or both with a TTL; **DAX** does the same job specifically for DynamoDB, sitting transparently in front of the table and answering `GetItem`, `BatchGetItem`, `Query`, and `Scan` calls from its own in-memory cache without any application changes to those calls -- a cache hit never touches DynamoDB, and every write-through operation (`PutItem`, `UpdateItem`, `DeleteItem`, `BatchWriteItem`) updates DynamoDB and DAX together and only succeeds if both writes succeed. Choose ElastiCache when the database being cached is relational (or when the cache must also serve as a general-purpose in-memory store outside the database path); choose DAX when the database being cached is DynamoDB and the workload is dominated by the same handful of hot keys re-read repeatedly.

**Exam tip:** "DynamoDB reads are the bottleneck and the read pattern is heavily skewed toward a few popular items" points to DAX; a relational database with the same symptom points to ElastiCache.

### Warnings

- Do not use the AWS root user for routine lab work.
- Stopping an instance is not teardown.
- $10 budget alerts warn; they do not stop spend.
